name: Korean exfoliating mitt
lead: The Korean exfoliating mitt, known in Korea as the Italy towel (idaeri taol), is a coarse viscose, sisal or nylon glove used to scrub the whole body, usually after soaking in warm water. The scrubbing rolls off the outer layer of dead skin in visible grey strands, and people use it to get smoother, softer-feeling skin and a fresher, more even look on the body.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that Kim Won-jo, CEO of Hanil Textile, invented the towel in Busan in 1967 and that it was named for the viscose fabric imported from Italy at the time; it became a household item in Korea and a staple of Korean saunas, and a 2017 poll by the Korean Intellectual Property Office ranked it among the country's top ten inventions.[1] Colour marks coarseness, with pink the softest, green the standard and blue the most coarse.[1]

The mitt is a form of mechanical exfoliation, which removes dead cells from the outermost skin layer, the stratum corneum.[2][3] Research specific to the mitt is limited to a 2002 study on how skin responds to mechanical injury of the stratum corneum.[4]

angle.text: The mitt physically sheds the top layer of dead skin cells, leaving the body feeling smoother and looking fresher for a while afterwards. Skin regrows its outer layer, so the look is repeated through regular bathing.

paras: Most Italy towels are two fabric squares sewn together to fit snugly over the hand, made of viscose rayon, sisal hemp or nylon.[1] Colour indicates strength, with green the standard and most common.[1] Use has spread from Korea to Thailand, northern China, Central Asia and Japan.[1]

Kim Won-jo of Hanil Textile invented the towel in Busan in 1967; the name refers to the Italian viscose fabric used then.[1] It became standard in Korean homes and in bathhouses such as jjimjilbang, which Wikipedia describes as Korean bathhouses that grew popular in the 1990s with hot tubs, saunas and massage areas.[1][5]

Wikipedia notes Vogue writer Monica Kim has recommended soaking or wetting skin for several minutes first and using a soothing soap before scrubbing.[1] Exfoliation removes dead cells from the stratum corneum, which is renewed continuously as cells move up from the basal layer.[2] Wikipedia's exfoliation article lists microfibre cloths, loofahs and brushes as mechanical exfoliants, and says benefits include removal of dead cells and build-up.[3]
No studies found of Korean exfoliating mitts as a product. A 2002 study examined biophysical changes after mechanical injury to the stratum corneum in normal skin.[4]

Korean scrub staff (ttaemiri) advise using the towel about once a week to avoid skin damage, according to Wikipedia.[1] Wikipedia's exfoliation article says dermatologists regard manual exfoliation as not medically necessary because dead skin sheds naturally, and that excessive exfoliation can weaken the skin barrier and cause tightness and sensitivity.[3] Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, likewise reports that aggressive physical exfoliation can cause irritation or aggravate acne.[2]
The mitt appears in body-care lists as an inexpensive full-body exfoliant. Community discussion specific to it was not found.
